learning_outcomes.text: The student will know the fundamental notions of solid-state physics, specifically of crystals. The student will possess the methodological tools to understand the essential microscopic and electronic mechanisms of metal physics, semiconductors, magnetic behaviors, and the superconducting state. The educational path will also provide basic knowledge of wave mechanics, atomic physics, and interatomic bonds, as well as the principles of some solid investigation techniques, which will allow them to address more specific problems of materials science that they may encounter during their career.

The student must demonstrate the ability to apply the notions developed in the course to solve problems concerning the crystalline composition of solids, their electronic, magnetic, and lattice properties. They must demonstrate the ability to interpret measurements of certain physical quantities or the results of specific measurement techniques in light of what was illustrated during the course, to derive information on the main characteristics of a material of interest for electronics.

The educational path is aimed at providing students with the critical capacity to recognize the level of approximation used for the microscopic description of certain properties of solids and the scope of applicability. The student must be able to evaluate the role of the hypotheses adopted for the development of a given model of solid-state and materials physics, and understand to what extent and within what limits the results are to be considered valid. They must also show the ability to apply certain concepts illustrated in the course to devices and investigation tools of interest for electronics and material studies. Students will be able to autonomously deepen the topics covered.

syllabus_topics: Sommerfeld model for metals: density of states and Fermi level
Ohm's law and mean free path
Response to alternating electric fields and plasma frequency
Effect of a periodic potential on crystal electrons
Electrical conductivity of doped semiconductors and Hall effect
Magnetic properties of atoms and solids: Hund's rules and ground state
Superconductivity: phenomenology and London and Pippard theories
Type I and type II superconductors and Ginzburg-Landau theory
Applications and measurement techniques: scanning probe and electron microscopies
assessment_rules: The exam consists of a written and an oral test. The written test, which is a prerequisite for the oral exam, is scheduled at the end of the course and includes free-response questions and numerical exercises. The written test provides a self-contained evaluation of the student. The oral exam, contingent on a positive outcome of the written test, may serve to modulate the grade obtained from the written test.
